study.title: Bangalore East: a thin rocky water reserve under a growing city
study.summary: The official groundwater health check for Bangalore East taluk: two thin hard-rock aquifers pumped far beyond refill, village wells mostly drinkable but nitrate-tainted, and a tentative plan of rain-catching structures and water-saving to ease pressure from 161% toward 142%.

timelines.title: Groundwater assessments 2013-2020: over-exploited throughout
timelines.description: Stage rises each assessment; category Over Exploited throughout.

target-study.analysis: This is the official Central Ground Water Board map and management plan for the groundwater under Bangalore East taluk, prepared under the National Aquifer Mapping project for 2020-21. Think of it as a health checkup plus a treatment plan for the underground water beneath this fast-growing corner of Bengaluru: it maps the rocks that hold water, measures how much is pumped versus refilled, flags pollution, and proposes small rain-catching structures and water-saving steps. Everything in this viewer comes from that one report.

target-layer-l-study-extent.analysis: Bangalore East is a young taluk — carved out of Bangalore South after the 2001 Census — covering 336 square kilometres with 5 hoblies and 173 villages and home to about one lakh people in 2011. It sits between fixed map coordinates, bordered by Bangalore South and North, Hoskote and Devanahalli, and Anekal. Because the city is expanding into it, farms are giving way to buildings — the backdrop for every water finding here.

target-layer-l-exploration-wells.analysis: Five test wells drilled across the taluk in 2021 tell one consistent story: the deep rock gives very little water, between 0.4 and 1.18 litres a second — about as much as a slowly dripping tap. Curiously, the shallowest well (Kalkere, 93 metres) is the best of the five, so drilling deeper did not help. These five points anchor the underground cross-sections.

target-layer-l-quality-sites.analysis: Six village wells sampled in 2018-19 show water that is mostly safe to drink except for nitrate, a fertiliser-and-sewage pollutant found too high in five of the six villages. Fluoride is low everywhere and hardness is a problem only in Avalahalli. A sixth village, K.Narayapura, keeps its lab results in the table but stays off the map because its printed location is garbled.

target-layer-l-check-dams.analysis: Fifteen small barriers called check dams are proposed across seasonal streams — from Sulakunte in the south to Jyothipura in the north. A check dam slows rainy-season runoff so it soaks underground instead of rushing away. Every site here is tentative: engineers must visit each stream and prepare a detailed estimate before anything is built.

target-layer-l-percolation-tanks.analysis: Three percolation tanks — shallow pond-like structures at Kodathi and Cheemasandra and J.I.Kada Agrahara — are proposed to hold monsoon water and let it seep down into the shallow aquifer. Like the check dams, these are shortlisted spots, not sanctioned construction sites.

target-layer-l-waterlevel-zones.analysis: In May 2018, before the rains, water sat just 2-5 metres below ground everywhere. After the monsoon, most of the taluk stayed that shallow, but a strip in the north stood deeper at 5-10 metres — the rains had refilled the south and centre more. In 2019 the rains lifted levels across the west most strongly, while one north-eastern pocket dipped slightly. Over the decade 2010-2019 the total change stayed under 2 metres, though the map does not say in which direction.

target-layer-l-recharge-feasible.analysis: Only parts of the taluk can usefully host recharge structures: a band in the north and a tip in the south, together 108 square kilometres, where about 2.9 million cubic metres of monsoon runoff could be caught. That is the entire canvas for the proposed dams and tanks — the built-up middle of the taluk is not considered suitable.

target-layer-l-thematic-basemaps.analysis: Seven theme maps set the scene. The land is mostly flat plains; buildings already blanket the north, east and south while farming hangs on in the west. The soil is clayey almost everywhere, and at map scale the whole taluk is one rock — banded gneiss. The weathered cover over that rock is mostly 20-30 metres thick, with the thickest pockets in the east, and village tanks dot the drainage map.

target-layer-l-sections.analysis: Slices through the ground show the same four-layer sandwich everywhere: topsoil, weathered rock that holds the shallow water, a thin cracked layer that holds the deep water, and solid basement rock. In one slice the cracked layer pinches out over a buried rock high — a picture of why deep wells here are so unreliable. The slices are structural sketches; the report prints no exact depth numbers on them.

target-ft-ew-immadahalli.analysis: Immadahalli's 200-metre test well struck water-bearing cracks at about 66 and 113 metres, yet yields only half a litre a second, and its resting water level sits 60 metres down — the deepest of the five wells. A thick 58-metre casing was needed through the loose top. It is a textbook case of this taluk: deep drilling, little reward.

target-ft-ew-bhattarahalli.analysis: Bhattarahalli's well passes through three separate crack zones — near 27, 82 and 146 metres — and still produces only half a litre a second, with water resting about 8.5 metres down. More cracks did not mean more water, which is why the report judges the deep aquifer unsustainable for long pumping.

target-ft-ew-kalkere.analysis: Kalkere is the star of a weak set: at just 93 metres it is the shallowest test well, yet its three crack zones deliver 1.18 litres a second — the highest yield recorded. Its water rests about 11 metres down. If any spot shows the deep rock at its best, it is here, and even here the flow is modest.

target-ft-ew-kodathi.analysis: Kodathi's 200-metre well found only two thin crack zones near 24 and 63 metres and yields three-quarters of a litre a second, with water resting about 19 metres down. Drilling past 60 metres added essentially nothing — the extra 140 metres of bore buy no extra water.

target-ft-ew-sadaramangala.analysis: Sadaramangala's well is the weakest at 0.4 litres a second despite four crack zones down to 169 metres — but it is also the most studied, because its water was laboratory-tested in two zones and passed every drinking-water check. Weak in quantity, clean in quality: that contrast is the taluk's story in one borewell.

target-ft-qw-doddakannahalli.analysis: Doddakannahalli's well water is drinkable on fluoride and hardness but carries 40 milligrams of nitrate per litre — close to the 45 limit and a warning sign of fertiliser or sewage seeping in. It needs watching, not alarm.

target-ft-qw-devarabeesanahalli.analysis: Devarabeesanahalli records the highest fluoride of the six villages at 0.44 milligrams per litre — still safely below the 1.0 limit — but its nitrate at 42 is near the edge. Soft water (hardness 172) otherwise.

target-ft-qw-mahadevapura.analysis: Mahadevapura's nitrate at 54 milligrams per litre clearly crosses the desirable limit, and its hardness at 576 is high though still within the permissible cap. This is one of the villages where the report's nitrate warning bites most.

target-ft-qw-avalahalli.analysis: Avalahalli is the worst-affected village sampled: hardness 820 milligrams per litre shoots past even the 600 permissible ceiling, and nitrate at 47 also breaches the desirable limit. Very hard water fur up pipes and vessels; paired with nitrate, this well deserves first attention for dilution and source control.

target-ft-qw-manduru.analysis: Manduru records the highest nitrate of all at 57 milligrams per litre — firmly above the desirable limit, likely from sewage or heavy fertiliser use nearby. Fluoride and hardness are otherwise acceptable. Cleaning up the nitrate sources around Manduru is squarely the report's prescription.

target_insights.analysis: This is the official Central Ground Water Board map and management plan for the groundwater under Bangalore East taluk, prepared under the National Aquifer Mapping project for 2020-21. Think of it as a health checkup plus a treatment plan for the underground water beneath this fast-growing corner of Bengaluru: it maps the rocks that hold water, measures how much is pumped versus refilled, flags pollution, and proposes small rain-catching structures and water-saving steps. Everything in this viewer comes from that one report.

Bangalore East is a young taluk — carved out of Bangalore South after the 2001 Census — covering 336 square kilometres with 5 hoblies and 173 villages and home to about one lakh people in 2011. It sits between fixed map coordinates, bordered by Bangalore South and North, Hoskote and Devanahalli, and Anekal. Because the city is expanding into it, farms are giving way to buildings — the backdrop for every water finding here.

Five test wells drilled across the taluk in 2021 tell one consistent story: the deep rock gives very little water, between 0.4 and 1.18 litres a second — about as much as a slowly dripping tap. Curiously, the shallowest well (Kalkere, 93 metres) is the best of the five, so drilling deeper did not help. These five points anchor the underground cross-sections.

Six village wells sampled in 2018-19 show water that is mostly safe to drink except for nitrate, a fertiliser-and-sewage pollutant found too high in five of the six villages. Fluoride is low everywhere and hardness is a problem only in Avalahalli. A sixth village, K.Narayapura, keeps its lab results in the table but stays off the map because its printed location is garbled.

Fifteen small barriers called check dams are proposed across seasonal streams — from Sulakunte in the south to Jyothipura in the north. A check dam slows rainy-season runoff so it soaks underground instead of rushing away. Every site here is tentative: engineers must visit each stream and prepare a detailed estimate before anything is built.

Three percolation tanks — shallow pond-like structures at Kodathi and Cheemasandra and J.I.Kada Agrahara — are proposed to hold monsoon water and let it seep down into the shallow aquifer. Like the check dams, these are shortlisted spots, not sanctioned construction sites.

In May 2018, before the rains, water sat just 2-5 metres below ground everywhere. After the monsoon, most of the taluk stayed that shallow, but a strip in the north stood deeper at 5-10 metres — the rains had refilled the south and centre more. In 2019 the rains lifted levels across the west most strongly, while one north-eastern pocket dipped slightly. Over the decade 2010-2019 the total change stayed under 2 metres, though the map does not say in which direction.

Only parts of the taluk can usefully host recharge structures: a band in the north and a tip in the south, together 108 square kilometres, where about 2.9 million cubic metres of monsoon runoff could be caught. That is the entire canvas for the proposed dams and tanks — the built-up middle of the taluk is not considered suitable.

Seven theme maps set the scene. The land is mostly flat plains; buildings already blanket the north, east and south while farming hangs on in the west. The soil is clayey almost everywhere, and at map scale the whole taluk is one rock — banded gneiss. The weathered cover over that rock is mostly 20-30 metres thick, with the thickest pockets in the east, and village tanks dot the drainage map.

Slices through the ground show the same four-layer sandwich everywhere: topsoil, weathered rock that holds the shallow water, a thin cracked layer that holds the deep water, and solid basement rock. In one slice the cracked layer pinches out over a buried rock high — a picture of why deep wells here are so unreliable. The slices are structural sketches; the report prints no exact depth numbers on them.

Immadahalli's 200-metre test well struck water-bearing cracks at about 66 and 113 metres, yet yields only half a litre a second, and its resting water level sits 60 metres down — the deepest of the five wells. A thick 58-metre casing was needed through the loose top. It is a textbook case of this taluk: deep drilling, little reward.

Bhattarahalli's well passes through three separate crack zones — near 27, 82 and 146 metres — and still produces only half a litre a second, with water resting about 8.5 metres down. More cracks did not mean more water, which is why the report judges the deep aquifer unsustainable for long pumping.

Kalkere is the star of a weak set: at just 93 metres it is the shallowest test well, yet its three crack zones deliver 1.18 litres a second — the highest yield recorded. Its water rests about 11 metres down. If any spot shows the deep rock at its best, it is here, and even here the flow is modest.

Kodathi's 200-metre well found only two thin crack zones near 24 and 63 metres and yields three-quarters of a litre a second, with water resting about 19 metres down. Drilling past 60 metres added essentially nothing — the extra 140 metres of bore buy no extra water.

Sadaramangala's well is the weakest at 0.4 litres a second despite four crack zones down to 169 metres — but it is also the most studied, because its water was laboratory-tested in two zones and passed every drinking-water check. Weak in quantity, clean in quality: that contrast is the taluk's story in one borewell.

Doddakannahalli's well water is drinkable on fluoride and hardness but carries 40 milligrams of nitrate per litre — close to the 45 limit and a warning sign of fertiliser or sewage seeping in. It needs watching, not alarm.

Devarabeesanahalli records the highest fluoride of the six villages at 0.44 milligrams per litre — still safely below the 1.0 limit — but its nitrate at 42 is near the edge. Soft water (hardness 172) otherwise.

Mahadevapura's nitrate at 54 milligrams per litre clearly crosses the desirable limit, and its hardness at 576 is high though still within the permissible cap. This is one of the villages where the report's nitrate warning bites most.

Avalahalli is the worst-affected village sampled: hardness 820 milligrams per litre shoots past even the 600 permissible ceiling, and nitrate at 47 also breaches the desirable limit. Very hard water fur up pipes and vessels; paired with nitrate, this well deserves first attention for dilution and source control.

Manduru records the highest nitrate of all at 57 milligrams per litre — firmly above the desirable limit, likely from sewage or heavy fertiliser use nearby. Fluoride and hardness are otherwise acceptable. Cleaning up the nitrate sources around Manduru is squarely the report's prescription.

report.source_title: Report on Aquifer Mapping and Management Plan, Bangalore East Taluk, Bangalore Urban District, Karnataka (CGWB, SWR, Bengaluru, July 2022)
report.display_title: Bangalore East: a thin rocky water reserve under a growing city
report.brief_description: The official groundwater health check for Bangalore East taluk: two thin hard-rock aquifers pumped far beyond refill, village wells mostly drinkable but nitrate-tainted, and a tentative plan of rain-catching structures and water-saving to ease pressure from 161% toward 142%.

blocks.headline: Pumping at 161% of refill in a 336 sq km urbanising taluk
blocks.content: Bangalore East is a young taluk on Bengaluru's eastern edge — 336 square kilometres, 5 hoblies, 173 villages, about one lakh residents in 2011 — being steadily built over. Its underground water lives in thin granite-and-gneiss rock that refills slowly, yet borewells pump out roughly one-and-a-half times what the rains put back, a deficit that has worsened every assessment since 2013. The official verdict is **Over Exploited**: nothing is left for new irrigation, and deep aquifers must now be reserved for drinking water. The way out proposed here is to catch more rain (18 structures, 218 ham), waste less water (153 ham), and police the aquifers — together pulling pressure from 161% back toward 142%.

blocks.headline: Flat clayey plains over one uniform hard rock
blocks.content: Most of the taluk is flat plains with small foothill patches in the north, and the soil is clayey almost everywhere (bonier skeletal soils only in the north-west). Buildings already dominate the north, east and south while farming survives in the west and centre — a land-use map of a city swallowing its fields. Underneath it all, at map scale, there is just one rock: banded gneiss, an ancient hard formation cut by dark dyke intrusions. Tanks and streams still criss-cross the drainage map, but the built-up middle is no longer considered worth recharging artificially — only a northern band and a southern tip, 108 square kilometres, are marked feasible.

metrics.label: Weathered cover
metrics.display_value: mostly 20-30 m thick, thickest in the east

blocks.headline: A shallow sponge over deep cracks — both thin
blocks.content: Water sits in two stacked stores. The shallow one (Aquifer-I) is the weathered, sponge-like top of the rock, roughly 2-58 metres thick, with water just 2-5 metres down — but it drains fast and cannot sustain long pumping. The deep one (Aquifer-II) is water trapped in cracks between 26 and 170 metres, yielding a meagre 0.5-1.2 cubic metres an hour for less than an hour at a time. Five test wells drilled in 2021 confirm the gloom: the best (Kalkere) gives 1.18 litres a second from 93 metres, the worst (Sadaramangala) 0.4 litres from 200 metres. Underground slices show why — a thin cracked layer that pinches out over buried rock highs.

blocks.headline: The rains refill the shallow layer — except in the stubborn north
blocks.content: 2020 was a kind year: 1,019 mm of rain against an 815 mm normal. Before the 2018 monsoon, water sat 2-5 metres down across the whole taluk; after it, most of the taluk stayed that shallow while a northern strip stood at 5-10 metres. The 2019 seasonal map shows the same geography — levels rose everywhere, most in the west, with only a north-eastern pocket dipping under 2 metres. Over the decade the total movement stayed below 2 metres, though the printed map frustratingly does not say whether that was up or down.

blocks.headline: Pumping at 161% — worse every single assessment
blocks.content: The numbers march one way: 134% in 2013, 155% in 2017, 161% in 2020, with draft (4,393 ham) far above refill (2,727 ham). All irrigation already comes from 1,234 private borewells watering 728 hectares, and the plan states plainly that no new irrigation area is possible — the city is paving the fields. The response is regulatory: the groundwater authority must notify aquifers below 100 metres for future drinking use only, and force rainwater harvesting and recharge into every new building.

blocks.headline: Safe to drink — except for nitrate, which stains the map
blocks.content: The deep test well at Sadaramangala passes every laboratory check in both sampled zones. Village wells are a shade worse: fluoride is low and safe everywhere (0.13-0.44), but nitrate crosses the desirable limit in five of six villages — Manduru worst at 57, Mahadevapura at 54 — and Avalahalli's hardness (820) even breaks the permissible ceiling. The report names nitrate, from sewage and nitrogen fertilisers, as the taluk's main quality problem, and prescribes diluting it through recharge plus village-level clean-up of sewage disposal. One village, K.Narayapura, keeps the cleanest nitrate reading (7) but its printed coordinates are gibberish, so its dot stays off the map.

blocks.headline: Catch more rain, waste less water: the path from 161% to 142%
blocks.content: The arithmetic is refreshingly concrete. Catch 2.9 million cubic metres of surplus runoff with 3 percolation tanks and 15 check dams (75% efficiency banks 218 ham) at a provisional cost of Rs 2.1 crore. Save 153 ham by putting drip and sprinkler irrigation on all 728 watered hectares. Together that is 371 ham, lifting available water to 3,098 ham and cutting pressure to 142%. Treated sewage (796 ham) cannot help — it is all piped away to Kolar and Chikballapur. Crop-switching is pointless (paddy is only 38 ha) and new irrigation impossible; discipline and maintenance of the structures carry the plan.

blocks.headline: What the report leaves fuzzy — read before you build
blocks.content: A few honest caveats. The text says four test wells but prints five, numbered 1, 2, 3, 6, 7 — a numbering slip, not missing wells. One intervention table prints '113 from 142' where the summary and text agree the recovery is 161% to 142%. The 70 village borewell depths carry no units, so they stay a table, not a depth chart. All 18 structure sites are tentative pending field visits, and the map-zone boundaries are figure approximations, not surveyed lines.
